newsitem.title: RUSSIA: WESTERN MAJORS EYE RUSSIAN ROSNEFT OIL COMPANY.
newsitem.headline: WESTERN MAJORS EYE RUSSIAN ROSNEFT OIL COMPANY.

text.p: International oil majors are ogling Russia's Rosneft oil company, one of the last large, state energy firms due to be sold off and a test case of Moscow's new resolve to make privatisation fairer.
"Shell and Exxon have been talking to Putilov (Rosneft's board chairman)," said Rosneft spokesman Vladimir Vyunitsky.

Shell (the U.S. unit of Royal Dutch/Shell) and Exxon could not immediately be reached for comment on whether they intended to buy a 51 percent Rosneft stake that will probably be sold off in September.

The forthcoming privatisation, which could bring in $1 billion to government coffers, is closely watched for signs of what Moscow says is a policy shift in the way it sells off its industrial crown jewels.
The sale of Rosneft, one of the oil sector's more comely catches, is a tangle of business and political forces jockeying for influence over the largest property sell-off in history.

Rosneft is a firm in need of foreign investment to flourish -- investment which could emerge only if Moscow makes good on a vow to sell off companies in a transparent and market-oriented way, and not to just seal sweet deals for insiders close to the government, analysts say.
Vyunitsky said the government might, for Rosneft only, scrap a law limiting foreign ownership in oil firms to 15 percent.

"You have to be allied with a major Russian element to win," said Dan Lubash, head of European emerging markets at Merrill Lynch. "I'm sure there will be strong interest among the major Russian groups and foreigners. Rosneft is a significant asset."

That fact has sparked keen interest from Russia's oligarchies, including, sources said, rival oil group SIDANKO, which is owned by Uneximbank, and Alfa-Group. "Quite a few consortiums are taking shape out there," said one source.
Vyunitsky said U.S. financier George Soros had approached State Property Fund former chairman Alfred Kokh about buying Rosneft for $1 billion.

But Vyunitsky said Rosneft wanted a long-term strategic partner from the energy world, adding the company would retain its unique status as the state's agent in production-sharing deals after the sale, possibly for up to three years.

Rosneft's ultimate fate will depend on whether oil producer Purneftegaz is part of the company when it is sold -- an issue to be resolved by the Supreme Court in early September and by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomydin.
Rosneft and SIDANKO both claim ownership of Purneftegaz.
Because Purneftegaz is key to Rosneft's value, it is a barometer of Moscow's resolve to use privatisation to raise money, as it did with the landmark Svyazinvest telecoms sale.
"The Rosneft sale is important in that it will show whether Svyazinvest is an exception or the beginning of a new era," said Russian-European Centre for Economic Policy's Rory MacFarquhar.

The Kremlin's promise of change comes after Maxim Boiko, a man highly experienced in the flotation of state-owned companies, became privatisation minister last week after Alfred Kokh resigned from the post.

Uneximbank, king of the privatisation mountain for its wins in the Svyazinvest and Norilsk Nickel metals group sales, will bid for Rosneft. So will Sibneft, the oil firm controlled by financier Boris Berezovsky and which handles Rosneft's exports.

Chances are good Rosneft will be sold with Purneftegaz, since reformist First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais and his ally, Fuel and Energy Minister Boris Nemtsov, have recommended the sale be structured that way.

Rosneft owns the Sakhalinmorneftegaz producer in the Russian Far East as well as three major refineries and stakes in major international oil deals, including a planned pipeline from Kazakhstan to Russia's Black Sea outlet of Novorossiisk.
"These projects will need a significant amount of capital," Lubash said. "Foreign participation will be crucial."
